synthesis.headline: Mature Great Lakes low drags Marginal-risk front through Southeast; interior ridge holds as Pacific trough deepens
synthesis.narrative:
Yesterday's occluding Midwest cyclone is now mature. Its surface low, about 996-998 mb, sits over far northwest Wisconsin under a closed 500 mb low near Lake Michigan (roughly 552-558 dam, core near -30 to -40 C). The cold front runs from northeast Illinois to a weak low over far eastern Louisiana, and satellite shows a convective band from the Ohio Valley through Mississippi, Alabama and western Georgia into the Florida Panhandle. Severe potential is low-end. SPC has a Marginal risk from Kentucky and Tennessee into northern Alabama and Georgia: isolated damaging gusts, and a brief tornado most plausible from northeast Alabama into north Georgia. MLCAPE is only near 1000 J/kg, lapse rates are poor and shear sits mostly below 700 mb. WPC has Marginal excessive-rain risks over the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians, and over southeast Florida, where heavy rain falls on ground flooded for several days. Thursday has no severe or excessive-rain area. In the West, an upper low leaving the Four Corners brings snow to Central Rockies peaks.

The flow is amplified and slow. A ridge over the Rockies and northern Plains, centered on Montana, sits northwest of the Great Lakes low; this is not a Rex block. A weak low (564-570 dam) lies beneath the ridge near Nevada and Utah, and an Atlantic ridge near 588 dam sits off the Carolinas. Squeezed between the ridges, the eastern low turns in place rather than moving off. Its surface low reaches western Quebec Thursday as the 50-65 kt jet streak at the trough's base heads for the Lower Great Lakes. Dewpoints in the 60s reach southern New England by Friday morning, with elevated storms from North Carolina to New Jersey overnight. Behind the front, a 1026 mb high over the northern Rockies and a second front cool the Heartland to slightly below normal for two days. An upper disturbance at the trough's southern end triggers a few elevated storms in Oklahoma Thursday.

From Saturday through next Wednesday, new disturbances diving in from the northern Plains keep the eastern trough in place. Expect showers from the Great Lakes to the Northeast, lake-effect snow or rain, and possibly a coastal low on an uncertain track. A southern-stream system brings storms to Texas and the western Gulf Coast. A deep northeast Pacific trough soaks the Northwest, and an atmospheric river may reach the West Coast early next week, with rain into California and strong winds. The Heartland chill does not break the interior ridge. CPC's 6-10 day mean keeps heights about 9 dam above normal over the interior, with 80-90% odds of above-normal temperatures on the northern Plains. At 8-14 days the warm core moves east into the northern Plains and central Canada, not toward the Southwest. The ridge pattern persists but moves east, and the West turns troughy.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong El Niño frames the season. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.46 C for ASO 2026, up from slightly negative in early 2026 and well past the +1.5 C strong threshold, though recent gains have slowed. The deep Gulf of Alaska trough in CPC's outlooks, and the southern-stream systems reaching Texas and the Gulf, fit the typical El Niño setup of a stronger Pacific jet and an active southern branch. With under four weeks left in hurricane season, no tropical cyclones are active. The Atlantic offers only a possible subtropical low, while the eastern and central Pacific remain more productive.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. Canada: a deep 973 hPa low over the Yukon and northwest BC (00Z analysis), and a 982 hPa low near Baffin Bay with tight isobars toward Greenland, meaning strong winds there. Tropics: a broad low south of Bermuda could turn subtropical (30% in 48 h, 50% in 7 days); EP95 is likely to become a depression southeast of Hawaii (70%); a low off Central America (50%) could bring heavy rain there.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z analysis (Wed Nov 4, 2026) is dominated by a deepening low of roughly 996-998 mb near the western Great Lakes, with a lobe of lower pressure (about 1004 mb) just to its east and a second low near 1009 mb over southern Quebec or the northern Maine border region. The main low drives a cold front south through the Mississippi Valley, plotted as a blue front running roughly from Wisconsin and Illinois down toward the Gulf Coast near Louisiana, where it appears to continue as a cold front or possible stationary extension offshore into the western Gulf. A warm front and associated occlusion arc east of the low toward Ontario and the Northeast, with a red/purple front line extending toward Maine, mark the northeastern portion of the system.

The tightest gradients appear in the Great Lakes and Upper Midwest around the 996-1006 mb low, where the isobars are closely spaced and the wind barbs look strongest. Slack gradients cover the southern Plains and Southeast behind and ahead of the front, and much of the interior West, where the pattern is a broad weak-pressure area with modest highs of roughly 1017-1018 mb over the Rockies and southern Plains. Those highs are unremarkable in strength and are not driving the weather here.

The strongest high on the chart is a 1026 mb center over the northern Rockies/Pacific Northwest interior, with another near 1026 mb off the Mid-Atlantic coast and a 1023 mb center near the Carolina coast. The northwest high is the only one with real cold-air-advection potential behind the departing system, though the chart alone does not show the temperature advection itself.

Lift and moisture appear focused along the cold front from the Mississippi Valley to the Gulf Coast, where dewpoints in the 60s and low 70s (degrees F) on the warm side contrast with 40s-50s behind it, and along the warm sector over the Southeast and Gulf states. A separate weak low (about 1010 mb) near the California-Nevada area and a trough in the Great Basin mark a second, weaker area of surface convergence in the West.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Wed 4 Nov 2026, is drawn on a polar projection, so the upper half of the frame is the Arctic Ocean, the Archipelago and Greenland rather than the provinces. The dominant feature over the Canadian landmass is a large, closed-isobar low of 973 hPa on the western side of the continent, with a second center of 977 hPa just to its north. Its closed circulation spans roughly the Yukon and northwestern British Columbia sector, and a trailing cold front sweeps south and then southwestward from the 973 center toward the Pacific, with a further front extending west into the Gulf of Alaska. A separate low of 995 hPa with its own frontal system sits over the far western Pacific edge of the chart, and a ridge of high pressure (1028 and 1026 hPa) lies between it and the continent.

Across the Canadian Archipelago and Baffin Bay region, several lows (982, 991, 997 and 1003 hPa) sit in a chain, with the 982 hPa low carrying a fronted circulation just west of Greenland's coast. A tight pressure gradient is evident on the eastern flank of that Baffin Bay low, where isobars crowd toward Greenland, implying a strong northerly or northwesterly flow there. Farther east, a 999 hPa low with a cold front trailing south sits over the Labrador Sea or Atlantic side, and a broad arc of high pressure (1025 to 1041 hPa) wraps the right edge of the chart.

Across the central and southern part of the map, a quasi-stationary east-west front runs from the northern Great Plains region toward the Great Lakes and Ontario/Quebec, with a 1006 hPa wave low near the upper Great Lakes and a 1004 hPa low over the central US. A cold front extends south from that wave toward the Gulf coast, and a series of high-pressure centers (1016 to 1023 hPa) fills the interior west and plains behind it. The arrangement shows a cold airmass backing into the central US while the active deep low and front sit upstream over northwestern Canada and the Pacific.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 1200 UTC 4 November 2026 analysis shows a high-amplitude, meridional pattern: a ridge over the Rockies and northern Plains, a deep closed low over the Great Lakes and upper Midwest, and a separate weak low over the interior West. The Great Lakes low, centered near the Michigan/Lake Michigan area, is closed with several concentric contours (roughly 552-558 dam), and the cold core (about -30 to -40 C) lines up with the height minimum. A colder trough axis extends southwestward through the Mississippi Valley toward Texas, with the implied jet corridor wrapping around the low's eastern and southern flank.

Along the Appalachians and Mississippi Valley, the strongest winds (shaded greens and olives, about 50-65 kt, with brown shading indicating still higher speeds) form a curved jet streak on the base and east side of the trough. The streak is oriented from southwest to northeast and curves cyclonically around the low, which is consistent with a negatively tilting wave, though the closed low itself carries little tilt. A second jet streak lies over the Southwest and southern California, oriented west-southwest to east-northeast along the southern flank of the western low.

The western low near the Nevada/Utah/Idaho region is a weaker closed circulation (heights around 564-570 dam), not clearly cut off from the westerlies to the south. The anticyclone symbol over Montana and the northern Rockies sits north-northwest of the Great Lakes low and well west of it, so this is not a Rex block: the high is neither directly poleward of the cutoff low nor at the same longitude. A better description is an amplified ridge to the northwest of a closed eastern low, with a separate western low beneath that ridge.

East of the trough, heights rise toward the Atlantic ridge, with the second high offshore of the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic coast near 588 dam, so the eastern low is confined between the western ridge and the Atlantic ridge. That squeeze, plus the closed circulation, suggests slow, retrograde-prone behavior and a low that pivots rather than translating quickly downstream. The overall flow is better described as quasi-blocked and slow-moving than progressive.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This 13:21Z Air Mass RGB on 4 November shows a north-south band of deep convection and thick cloud stretching from the Great Lakes/Ohio Valley region southward through the Mississippi and Alabama area into the Florida Panhandle and the northeastern Gulf. The brightest white, vigorous-looking cloud tops cluster over Mississippi, Alabama and western Georgia, with a trailing line extending south into the Florida peninsula and a thinner streak running southwest over the Gulf. This reads as a frontal or squall-line-type axis, and the sharp airmass contrast along its western edge marks the likely corridor of the upper flow.

West of that band, a broad orange-brown dry region covers the Plains and Mississippi Valley, with more saturated red-orange patches over the northern Rockies and northern Plains and across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes. Those darker red areas, partly wrapped in cloud, sit on the cyclonic side of the flow and are the most credible candidates for compact, higher-PV dry intrusions, though the image alone does not establish descent. Over the northern Great Lakes and southern Canada a cyclonic comma-like cloud and dry-slot structure is visible, suggesting a mature system there. Deep blue and purple tones along the far northwest edge of the image, over the Pacific off British Columbia and Washington, indicate cold dry upper-tropospheric air.

Off the Southeast coast, a distinct dry (orange-brown) swirl sits west of a large cloud shield over the western Atlantic. Its cyclonic curl around the edge of the cloud mass suggests a separate, likely vertically stacked system, with the dry air wrapping into its southwestern flank.

Green, moist tropical air dominates Mexico, the western Gulf and the Caribbean, with scattered convective clusters over Hispaniola, Cuba's southern waters and the southwestern Caribbean. A sharp edge of cirrus and a color gradient running from the Bahamas toward the Greater Antilles marks a boundary between the dry Atlantic air and the moist tropics, plausibly aligned with a subtropical jet corridor. The broad dry orange over the Gulf and Texas is dry upper-level air, not clearly an intrusion.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This 13:10Z GOES-19 Air Mass RGB (4 Nov) shows a broad tropical moist-air (green) expanse over the Caribbean, Central America, and both adjacent ocean basins, with the clearest organized convection in three places: a white, banded cloud shield over the western Atlantic roughly east of Bermuda's latitude, a cluster of bright cold-topped cells over the eastern Pacific south of Mexico, and a large, intense convective mass over southern Brazil and the adjacent Atlantic near the southern edge of the Brazilian border region. The Atlantic cloud shield has curved, comma-like cirrus streaming northeast from a dark orange-brown dry slot near 35N, which reads as a mature extratropical cyclone with a dry intrusion wrapping into it; the dark orange-brown there is the sharpest dry-air signature in the northern hemisphere in this frame.

Farther north, the polar jet and airmass boundary show up as the transition from green to blue and purple across eastern Canada and the northwest Atlantic, with a bright white cloud band along the northeast limb of the disk (off Labrador and the Canadian Maritimes) marking a frontal cloud band implied along the jet corridor. The deep purple and red tones over Hudson Bay and the Arctic fringe are the cold, dry, likely stratosphere-influenced air on the cyclonic side of that flow, though limb distortion makes precise placement there uncertain. Over Canada's interior, a pale pink-white cloud swath near the Great Lakes and Ontario shows a frontal band extending south into the eastern U.S.

Tropically, a thin whitish arc stretches from the Greater Antilles southwest toward Central America and northern Colombia, consistent with a convergence or frontal remnant, while scattered convective clusters sit over Colombia and Venezuela. Over the eastern tropical Pacific, large bright clouds at far left and the cluster south of Mexico suggest active ITCZ convection, with no obvious closed tropical cyclone circulation visible at this scale. The pronounced orange-brown band stretching across the southeast Pacific and Atlantic near 20S to 30S reads as dry subsident air rather than a stratospheric intrusion, given its broad, diffuse character.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
The outlook for November 9-13 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the contiguous US, with the strongest signal centered on the northern Plains. The darkest shading, 80-90% odds of above normal, covers North Dakota, South Dakota, eastern Montana and northern Nebraska, with 70-80% extending through the northern Rockies, Great Basin, upper Midwest and central Plains. Probabilities step down gradually southward and eastward, with 60-70% over California, the Southwest, and the mid-Mississippi Valley, and 50-60% across the southern Rockies, Texas Panhandle and Ohio Valley.

The Southeast and Atlantic Coast are where the signal fades: the leaning-above categories (33-50%) run from Texas and the Gulf Coast northeastward through the Tennessee Valley, Appalachians, and interior Northeast, and a near-normal band hugs the Gulf Coast, Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas, and the coastal Northeast. No below-normal area appears anywhere in the lower 48. In Alaska, below-normal odds (33-40%) cover the far western coast and Bering Sea side, near-normal sits in the interior, and above-normal strengthens eastward toward the Panhandle; Hawaii leans above normal.

The pattern is a warm anomaly with a maximum over the north-central US that decays toward the Atlantic seaboard, with no cold counterpart over the lower 48. That is consistent with, though not proof of, a persistent ridge or at least a lack of strong troughing over the western and central US, with a mean trough or milder flow stopping the warmth short of the East Coast. Note that these are probabilities of category, not magnitudes, so the 80-90% area signals confidence rather than extreme warmth. Because the chart shows no cold signal anywhere in the lower 48, it gives no hint of a regime breakdown within this window. Whether the ridge would break down after day 10 is not something this chart can address, though the sharp east-west gradient in confidence suggests the forecast tools disagree most about the eastern trough's position.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook, made 3 Nov 2026 and valid 9-13 Nov. Height contours are labeled in meters (5340 to 5880 m, i.e. about 534 to 588 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are at 60 m (6 dam) intervals with labels such as 30, 90 and -30, which look like meters; I read the largest positive values as roughly 90 m (about 9 dam), though the labels are small and that is my best reading.

The dominant positive anomaly is a broad area of red dashed contours over the interior of western and central North America, centered roughly over the northern Rockies and Plains and extending north into the Canadian prairies, with the 90 m (about 9 dam) label near the Great Lakes-Midwest. A second positive center sits over the Arctic Ocean north of Alaska and the Beaufort Sea, near the 5160 contour, with the 30 m (about 3 dam) label nearby. Negative anomalies (blue dashed) are strongest over the eastern North Pacific and Gulf of Alaska, with labels near -150 and -210 m (about -15 to -21 dam), and a weaker negative center near Hudson Bay and Quebec labeled about -30 m (about -3 dam).

The height contours show a deep trough anchored off the West Coast over the eastern Pacific, with strongly packed contours curving along the coast of British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest. Downstream, the ridge axis runs roughly from the southern Plains and Rockies north-northeastward toward the Canadian prairies and Hudson Bay region, then the contours turn sharply back southeast over eastern Canada. A trough is implied over the Northeast and Atlantic Canada, consistent with the blue center near Quebec.

On amplification, the 6-10 day mean shows a clear wave pattern rather than zonal flow. The positive anomalies cover the interior of western North America and the zero line (purple dashed) lies west of the Rockies, so only the immediate West Coast sits under negative anomalies. The ridge is not retreating from the interior in this outlook; with the Pacific trough upstream and the eastern trough downstream, the pattern appears to favor persistence of a western-interior ridge. A single outlook cannot show trend, so whether the ridge is strengthening or shrinking over time would need the preceding outlooks for comparison.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb height and height-departure outlook, made 3 November 2026 and valid 11-17 November. Solid green contours are mean heights, labeled in meters (5340 through 5820 on the southern edge, i.e. 534-582 dam), and dashed lines are departures at 60 m intervals, red positive and blue negative. A broad positive anomaly sits over central and eastern Canada and the northern tier of the US. The red contours center over the northern Plains and Upper Midwest, near the Dakotas and Minnesota, with the 90 m contour (about +9 dam) closed there and extending northward into Manitoba, Ontario and Hudson Bay. The ridge in the height contours is more of a broad northward bulge than a sharp axis, with the 5580 and 5640 lines pushed well north across the central US and southern Canada.

Over western Canada and the northern Rockies the picture is mixed. The positive anomaly does not extend over the Pacific Northwest or the Canadian Rockies; the 0 contour runs roughly along the Rockies and the blue negative contours start west of it. So the ridge core is centered over the northern Plains and central Canada rather than over the northern Rockies or toward the Southwest and northern Mexico, which look near-normal to slightly negative.

The strongest negative departures are over the Gulf of Alaska and the northeast Pacific, with minus 150 m (about -15 dam) contours near the British Columbia and Alaska Panhandle coast, producing tight height gradients and strong westerly flow into the West Coast. A second, weaker negative center lies over the northwest Atlantic near Newfoundland and the Labrador Sea, near -90 to -30 m. A positive center also appears over the Arctic north of Canada and again near Greenland and Baffin Island, so the high-latitude pattern is a strong Pacific trough upstream of a positive-anomaly ridge extending from the Plains to the Arctic.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: Only one category appears on this Day 1 outlook (valid 12Z Wed Nov 4 to 12Z Thu Nov 5, 2026): Marginal, the lowest tier, drawn in green. No Slight, Moderate or High areas are plotted. The larger Marginal area stretches across the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians, covering roughly central and eastern Tennessee, northern Georgia and Alabama, and extending northeast into eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia and western North Carolina, with its northern edge reaching toward southern Ohio and West Virginia. A second, much smaller Marginal area sits over extreme southern Florida near the southern tip of the peninsula, with the label partly over the coast and adjacent waters. Since both areas carry the same lowest category, neither holds a higher risk than the other. The chart shows only risk categories, not the cause, so I cannot tell from it whether these areas stem from a front or a tropical system. The elongated southwest-to-northeast orientation of the main area is at least consistent with a boundary or moisture axis, and its placement over higher terrain suggests the Appalachians may play a role, but both readings are inferences rather than anything the chart states.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: No risk area is drawn anywhere on this chart. The only text over the contiguous United States states that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent, which is below the Marginal threshold (at least 5 percent), so none of the four categories (Marginal, Slight, Moderate, High) appears. The outlook is valid 12Z Thursday November 5 through 12Z Friday November 6, 2026, and was issued at 0807Z Wednesday November 4. With no shaded polygons anywhere, from the Pacific Northwest to the Gulf Coast to the Northeast, the chart shows no region where flash flooding is considered even a low-end concern for this period. Because there is no Day 1 chart here for comparison, I can't say whether this represents a relaxation of earlier risk or simply a continuation of a quiet pattern. The chart supports only the statement that heavy-rain flash flood potential is minimal nationwide for this window.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 3 AM EST Wednesday, November 4, 2026, valid through 12Z Friday, November 6:

A trailing cold front tracks toward the Ohio Valley and Southeast, with showers and storms along it for several days and steady rain around a surface low over the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes. Impacts are generally limited, though isolated heavy rain and severe storms are possible today in the Lower Ohio Valley and Southeast. Locally heavy rain may persist along the southeast Florida coast today, a flash flood concern for an area still vulnerable from several days of flooding. Rain tapers off after today.

In the West, an upper low from the Four Corners brings increasing snow to the Central Rockies peaks. An emerging front tomorrow spreads precipitation to lower elevations of the Central and Southern High Plains and reinforces cold air, so Heartland temperatures fall to slightly below normal over the next two days. A weakening Pacific front brings modest low-elevation rain and mountain snow to the Northwest, with limited impacts expected.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
As of 0657 AM CST Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the SPC has a Marginal Risk (the lowest category) of severe thunderstorms for parts of the Southeast into the southern Appalachians, valid through 12Z November 5. Hazards are isolated severe wind gusts and a low-probability brief tornado.

A mature cyclone over the western MN/IA border is driving the pattern. Its surface low sits over far northwest WI, with a cold front extending southeast into far northeast IL and south to a low over far eastern LA. Mid-60s dewpoints extend through western KY, and thunderstorms are expected along and ahead of the front. Coverage is highest from central and eastern KY across middle and eastern TN into northern AL and GA.

Buoyancy is limited, with MLCAPE near 1000 J/kg, poor lapse rates, and widespread cloud cover. Moderate shear is mostly confined below 700 mb. The tornado threat is greatest from northeast AL across northern GA, where stronger surface southeasterlies are possible. Convectively aided damaging gusts are also possible across the region.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past six hours. Storm Prediction Center is not actively monitoring any organized convective threat at this time. Mesoscale discussions are issued when forecasters see a specific short-term area where watch issuance or a convective outlook update may be needed, so their absence means no such area is under active analysis. This does not rule out severe weather. Conditions can change quickly, and new discussions could be issued at any time if a developing threat emerges.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 700 AM EST Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the Atlantic outlook covers a broad low forming along a remnant front a few hundred miles south of Bermuda. It could gradually acquire subtropical characteristics through the weekend while moving slowly east over the western and central subtropical Atlantic. Conditions are expected to become unfavorable for further development by early next week. Formation chance is 30 percent through 48 hours (low) and 50 percent through 7 days (medium). Gale Warnings are in High Seas Forecasts.

As of 400 AM PST Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the East Pacific outlook has two areas. The first, EP95, lies well southeast of Hawaii, where a tropical depression is likely to form over the Central Pacific in the next few days. It would move west to west-northwest at 10 to 15 mph. Formation chance is 50 percent through 48 hours (medium) and 70 percent through 7 days (high). The second is a broad low offshore Central America producing disorganized showers and storms. A tropical depression could form by the weekend as it drifts north, with heavy rain possible over parts of Central America. Formation chance is 30 percent through 48 hours (low) and 50 percent through 7 days (medium).

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary: NHC currently lists no active tropical cyclones, and no advisories are being issued. The product gives no as-of time, so this status should be treated as unverified for the time of your briefing.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ENSO is in El Niño. The Oceanic Niño Index anomaly has risen every season in this table, from -0.21°C for JFM 2026 (near neutral and slightly cool) to +0.11°C for FMA, +0.46°C for MAM, +0.95°C for AMJ, +1.39°C for MJJ, +1.80°C for JJA, +2.16°C for JAS, and +2.46°C for ASO 2026. The most recent value, +2.46°C, is well above the +1.5°C threshold usually used for a strong event. The absolute Niño-region total has also climbed, from 26.57 to 29.23, with the rate of increase slowing somewhat in the latest seasons (JJA to JAS to ASO gains of about 0.07 and 0.11 in the total, alongside anomaly gains of 0.36 and 0.30). The product gives no as-of date and does not indicate which seasons are observed and which are forecast, so the timing of the latest values cannot be confirmed from this text alone.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices (CPC), latest values dated 2026-09-30. All three indices are stale: the newest value is 35 days old, and CPC has not updated the table, so none should be treated as current.

PNA: +0.12 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is -0.41, up from -1.51 the prior week, so the index has risen toward neutral after a strongly negative stretch, which would have favored eastern North American troughing.

AO: -0.26 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is +0.04, down from +1.73 the prior week, a falling trend that moved from clearly positive toward neutral-to-negative.

NAO: -0.78 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is -0.15, down from +0.28, and the index is falling toward negative values.

These are observed summer values. Extratropical teleconnections are weaker and less canonical in summer, so treat them as directional support only, not as standalone evidence.
